rationale: Proverbs identifies Solomon as David's son and Israel's king; Kings records Solomon taking the throne of his father David, supplying the royal family setting of this attribution.
The opening purpose is to know wisdom and discipline and understand sensible words; the later proverb directs the heart to discipline and the ears to words of discernment.
The book promises instruction in righteousness and right judgment; chapter 2 describes understanding righteousness and judgment as the outcome of receiving wisdom.
The stated aim of understanding righteousness and directing judgment has a concrete counterpart in Solomon's request to judge the people in righteousness and God's gift of a discerning, wise heart.

Proverbs aims to give shrewdness to the innocent and perception and thought to a young child; the psalm says the disclosure of God's words gives light and understanding to the simple. Both link instruction with perception or understanding while preserving the different descriptions of its recipients.
Both sayings describe growth in an already wise hearer: the wise listener becomes wiser here, and the wise person given a starting point receives more wisdom in chapter 9.
Understanding comparisons, obscure sayings and riddles is paired with the sage's study of parables, hidden meanings of proverbs and their riddles in Sirach.
Both passages call fear of the Lord the beginning of wisdom and associate good understanding with practicing it; the shared formulation links reverence with enacted understanding.
The book later repeats the principle that fear of the Lord begins wisdom, connecting the opening statement with the counsel of holy ones in chapter 9.
The paired commands to heed a father's instruction and not reject a mother's ordinances recur in chapter 6, preserving the distinctive instruction from both parents.
Both passages picture received wisdom as a crown of graces placed on the learner's head; the promised collar here and crown of delight there expand the image of honored instruction.
The warning not to consent when ungodly men invite the son is reinforced by the later command not to enter ungodly ways or imitate lawless conduct.

Both speeches put a collective plan against a righteous person into the plotters' mouths: Proverbs proposes unjust bloodshed, while Wisdom develops an ambush ending in torture and a shameful death sentence.

The robbers boast of swallowing someone alive like Hades; Numbers describes the earth swallowing the rebels and their descent alive to Hades. The shared image connects a murderous boast with the account of divine judgment.
The plan to seize costly property and fill houses with spoils parallels Micah's condemnation of coveting fields and plundering a man, his house and his inheritance.
The invitation to cast one's lot with plunderers and share their purse is paired with the psalm's condemnation of running with a thief and placing one's portion among wrongdoers.
Turning one's foot away from the criminals' paths corresponds to the blessed person's refusal to walk in ungodly counsel or stand in the way of sinners.
Both passages describe feet running toward evil and being quick to shed blood, making the same bodily image a description of readiness for violence.
Romans includes feet swift to pour out blood in its scriptural description of sinfulness, closely matching Proverbs' feet quick to shed blood.
The murderers store up evils for themselves; the psalm depicts the wrongdoer falling into his own pit and his injustice returning upon his head. Both locate the harm's return upon its planner.
The warning that lawless acquisition costs its practitioners their own life is paired with the later saying that taking bribes destroys the taker.
Wisdom speaks openly in the squares here; chapter 8 places her at paths and rulers' gates and has her send her voice to humankind. Both present wisdom as publicly accessible instruction.
Wisdom's position at rulers' and city gates recurs in chapter 8, where she sits beside rulers' gates and is praised at the entrances.
The speech's accusation that the senseless hated perception is resumed by the later explanation that they hated wisdom and refused fear of the Lord.
Wisdom promises to send forth an utterance and teach her word; her later speech invites listeners to hear the upright, truthful and righteous words proceeding from her lips.
Wisdom describes repeatedly calling without obedience; Isaiah's judgment likewise answers the failure to obey when the Lord called and the disregard shown when He spoke.
Ignoring wisdom's counsel and reproof corresponds to the sinner's hatred of instruction and casting God's words behind him in the psalm's rebuke.
Wisdom's laughter at the rejecters' ruin parallels the heavenly Lord's laughter and scorn before speaking in anger to rebellious rulers. Both use derision to announce judgment upon resistance.
The sudden overthrow arriving like a storm is paired with the later proverb in which the passing storm removes the impious while the righteous is saved.
Both passages announce that wrongdoers will cry for help and receive no hearing; Micah explicitly links the refusal to their wicked treatment of others.
The rejecters refuse wisdom and fear of the Lord; Job defines reverence for God as wisdom, clarifying the connection between the two things they reject.
The refusal to attend to counsel and the sneering at reproof repeat the earlier accusation of making counsel ineffective and disobeying reproof within Wisdom's speech.
Eating the fruit of one's own way is paired with reaping what one sows; Galatians makes the adverse harvest explicit as corruption from sowing into the flesh.
Proverbs says those who wronged the innocent will themselves be murdered; the psalm depicts attackers drawing weapons against the upright and then calls for their own sword to enter their heart.
Listening to Wisdom promises fearless rest here; chapter 3 develops secure sitting and sleep, freedom from sudden fright and the Lord's support along one's ways.
Receiving and hiding the commandment within oneself corresponds to the psalmist hiding God's sayings in his heart so that he may not sin.

The earlier assurance that the ear will obey wisdom and the learner will apply the heart to understanding corresponds to the later commands to apply the ear to the father's words and keep them in the heart.
Proverbs urges the learner to call and give voice for wisdom and understanding; James directs the person lacking wisdom to ask God, who gives it generously.
Seeking wisdom as silver and treasures is complemented by the later valuation of trading in wisdom above treasures of gold and silver.
Finding knowledge of God and understanding fear of the Lord is paired with Job's definition of reverence as wisdom and abstention from evil as knowledge.
Both passages expressly locate wisdom's gift in God: the Lord gives wisdom here, and James promises God's generous giving to the person who asks for it.
The statement that the Lord gives wisdom is illustrated by His response to Solomon's request for understanding: He gives Solomon a discerning and wise heart.

The Lord will shield the journey of those acting rightly; the psalm says the Lord directs a person's steps and supports his hand so that when he falls he will not be dashed down. Both connect divine care with the person's course and protection from harm.
Protecting the way of those who revere God is paired with the Lord guarding the person's soul and every coming in and going out in the ascent song.
The promised understanding of righteousness and judgment realizes the book's announced purpose of understanding true righteousness and directing judgment rightly.
Wisdom entering the learner's mind and perception pleasing the soul is paired with the later statement that wisdom is in a person's good heart.
Good counsel and holy thought guard the learner here; the later exhortation promises that wisdom will hold fast to and keep the person who loves and retains her.
Rescue from the evil way and an untrustworthy speaker corresponds to the condemned combination of an unjust tongue, feet hastening to harm and a witness kindling falsehoods.
Abandoning straight ways to walk in darkness is paired with the description of ungodly ways as dark and their travelers as unaware how they stumble.
Delight and rejoicing in evil correspond to the fool doing evil things in laughter in chapter 10. Both portray pleasure in wrongdoing; the later proverb explicitly identifies its subject as a fool.
The description of crooked paths and bent tracks is paired with the psalm's people turning aside into tangled ways and being led away with workers of lawlessness.
Being drawn away from a straight way and righteous judgment contrasts with Wisdom walking in righteousness and in paths of just judgment in her later speech.
Evil counsel abandons youthful teaching and forgets a divine covenant; the psalm recounts instruction passed from fathers to sons and then the failure to keep God's covenant or walk in His law.
The house beside death and courses beside Hades with the earthborn correspond to the foolish woman's setting where earth-born ones perish and her visitor reaches Hades' ledge.
The travelers' failure to return or reach life-giving straight paths is paired with the later warning about many murdered victims and a house whose ways descend to Hades and death's chambers.
The missed prospect of finding smooth righteous paths through walking good paths is paired with the father's teaching of wisdom's ways and leading onto straight tracks.
Both passages connect righteousness with lasting residence in the land: the good and innocent remain here, and the righteous inherit and dwell upon it in the psalm.

Proverbs says the ways of the ungodly will perish from the land and the lawless will be driven out of it. The psalm likewise says the lawless will be driven out, while distinguishing the guarding of God's holy ones and the destruction of the offspring of the ungodly.
The prohibition on forgetting ordinances and the call to keep words in the heart recur in the instruction to keep commandments and not forget or disregard the father's utterance.
The promise of longer life and peace through keeping instruction corresponds to walking God's commanded way so that life in the inherited land may be prolonged and go well.

Mercy and faithfulness are to be fastened around the neck here; the later instruction collars parental laws around the neck and fastens them upon the soul. Both picture what should govern conduct as something worn around the neck.
Taking thought for good things before the Lord and people corresponds to Paul's care to do what is honorable before both the Lord and people while administering the gift.
The command to take thought for good before people is echoed in Paul's command to take thought for what is honorable before all people, within his instruction against repaying evil.
Trusting God with the whole heart corresponds to Jeremiah's blessing of the person whose trust and hope are in the Lord, pictured as a well-watered tree secure in drought.
The prohibition on exalting oneself in one's own wisdom is paired with the later contrast between trusting a rash heart, which is folly, and walking in wisdom, which brings safety.
The assurance of straight ways and a foot that will not stumble is resumed in the promise of confident, peaceful walking without stumbling after the renewed call to keep counsel.
The warning not to be prudent in one's own estimation corresponds closely to Paul's command not to become wise in one's own eyes.

relationship: fear of God and departure from evil
rationale: The paired commands to fear God and turn from evil correspond to Job's paired definitions of reverence as wisdom and abstaining from evil as knowledge.
Healing for the body and care for the bones is paired with the later description of the father's words as life and healing for all flesh.
Honoring the Lord with firstfruits from righteous labor corresponds to the command to bring the first produce of the land into the Lord's house.
The promised filling of storerooms with grain corresponds to the covenant blessing sent upon storerooms and the work of the people's hands in the land.
Hebrews quotes the filial warning against making light of the Lord's discipline or fainting under His reproof, applying the exhortation to its hearers' endurance.
Hebrews reproduces the reason for receiving discipline: the Lord disciplines the one He loves and scourges every son He receives.
The blessing of the person who finds wisdom is paired with Wisdom's later blessing of the hearer who keeps her ways, which lead to life and favor from the Lord.
Trading in wisdom exceeds gold and silver; Job likewise denies that treasure, weighed silver or gold can purchase or equal wisdom.
Wisdom's greater value in trade is echoed when she describes her harvest as better than gold and precious stone and her produce as better than choice silver.
Wisdom's worth above costly stones is paired with Job's refusal to weigh wisdom against precious onyx, sappheiros, gold or golden vessels.
Wealth and glory in Wisdom's left hand correspond to her later declaration that wealth and glory belong to her, alongside possession of many things and righteousness.

Wisdom's gifts of years, wealth and glory have a concrete counterpart in God's gifts of wealth and glory to Solomon and His conditional promise to multiply Solomon's days if he keeps the commandments.
Wisdom carries law and mercy on her tongue; the final portrait joins a woman's wise, lawful speech with mercy that raised up her children. Both bring lawful speech and merciful conduct together.
Wisdom's good ways and peaceful paths correspond to the assurance that God will straighten the learner's tracks and advance the journey in peace.
Wisdom is a tree of life for those holding her; the later proverb says a tree of life grows from the fruit of righteousness. Both apply the life-bearing tree image to the moral life.
Both passages associate God's establishment of the earth with wisdom and His preparation or stretching out of heaven with understanding.
The declaration that God founded earth and prepared heaven by wisdom is developed in Wisdom's account of being beside Him as heaven, clouds, springs and earth's foundations were prepared.
Divine perception is linked here to the deeps and clouds; Wisdom's later creation account places her beside God as He establishes clouds, the world's springs and the earth's foundations.
The call not to drift away but keep counsel and thought corresponds to taking hold of discipline, refusing to release it and keeping it for one's life.
Grace around the neck, promised alongside life here, recalls the opening promise of a crown of graces and a golden collar received through instruction.
This continuation unit repeats the chapter's earlier assurance of healing for the body and care for the bones, preserving the renewed bodily-healing promise as its own source unit.
Confident walking without stumbling is paired with the later promise that one's steps will not be shut in while walking and one will not grow weary while running.
Fearless sitting and pleasant sleep correspond to the psalmist's resolve to lie down and sleep in peace because the Lord made him dwell alone in hope.

Freedom from approaching fright and ungodly assaults is paired with the righteous person's lack of fear at an evil report and established heart, with the assurance that he will not fear until he looks upon his enemies.
The Lord's support of the foot so it is not shaken corresponds to the command not to give one's foot over to shaking and the assurance of the wakeful Lord as keeper and shelter.

relationship: material help for a person in need
rationale: Helping when one's hand has the means corresponds to John's challenge to a person who has worldly goods yet closes the heart to a needy brother, followed by the call to love in deed.
Sending a needy person away while help can be given is paired with sending an unclothed or hungry brother or sister away with peaceful words but without providing bodily necessities.
The reason against delaying help until tomorrow is repeated in the later warning not to boast of tomorrow, because one does not know what the coming day will bear.
The warning against devising evil against a trusting neighbor is paired with the psalm's enemies planning harm and the treachery of a trusted companion who ate the speaker's bread.
Avoiding vain enmity lest harm follow corresponds to the later warning against rushing into battle and provoking enduring reproach and enmity, followed by counsel to seek reconciliation.
The command not to imitate evil men's ways is repeated in the prohibition on entering ungodly ways or imitating the lawless.
The lawless person's absence from the council of the righteous corresponds to the psalm's declaration that sinners will not rise in the righteous council.
The curse upon ungodly houses and blessing upon righteous dwellings correspond to the later contrast between impious houses disappearing and upright tents standing.
James introduces the same opposition of God to the proud and gift of grace to the humble as scriptural support for humility and submission to God.
First Peter quotes the proud-and-humble contrast while urging mutual humility, retaining God's opposition to pride and His grace toward the humble.
The wise inheriting glory corresponds to Sirach's promise that the person holding Wisdom fast will inherit glory and receive the Lord's blessing.
The summons for children to hear a father's discipline resumes the book's opening summons to the son to listen to his father's discipline.
The father calls his law a good gift and urges its retention; the psalm values the law from God's mouth above thousands of gold and silver. Both emphasize instruction's worth to the recipient.
The speaker recalls being a son obedient to his father; in the Solomonic setting supplied by Proverbs 1:1, Kings describes Solomon walking in his father David's ordinances.
The father teaches the child to let the word take hold in the heart; Deuteronomy places the commanded words in heart and soul and directs their teaching to sons.
Keeping commandments and refusing to forget the father's utterance restates the earlier appeal not to forget his ordinances but to keep his words in the heart.
Wisdom holds fast to the person who loves and keeps her; Sirach likewise says Wisdom takes hold of her seekers and that loving her is loving life.
Proverbs joins fortifying and honoring Wisdom with her promised exaltation and embrace; Sirach describes Wisdom raising her sons high and states that the person holding her fast will inherit glory.
The promised crown of graces on the learner's head repeats the earlier crown of graces received through parental instruction.
Receiving the father's words so that years of life multiply recalls the earlier promise that keeping his words adds length of life and years of living.
The multiplication of years through receiving instruction parallels God's promise to multiply Solomon's days if he walks in God's way and keeps His commandments as David did.
Teaching wisdom's ways and leading onto straight tracks corresponds to the earlier promised understanding of righteousness and judgment that makes good courses straight.
Running without growing weary is promised both to the learner led in wisdom's ways and to those enduring for God in Isaiah's renewal-of-strength passage.
Holding discipline for one's life corresponds to the later description of correction and discipline as life's way, alongside the law's commandment as lamp and light.
Not entering ungodly ways corresponds to the blessed person's refusal to walk in ungodly counsel or stand in sinners' way.
Avoiding the place where wrongdoers encamp corresponds to the psalmist's refusal to enter with transgressors or sit with an assembly of evildoers.

relationship: wrongdoing around the time of rest
rationale: Proverbs depicts people unable to sleep without doing harm; Micah depicts people planning evil on their beds and carrying it out at daybreak. Both join habitual wrongdoing to the setting of rest.
Drinking lawless wine is paired with Eliphaz's depiction of the unclean person drinking injustice as a drink; both portray wrongdoing through the act of consuming liquid.
The righteous person's ways shine and advance toward day; the psalm declares that light has dawned for the righteous and gladness for the upright in heart.
The righteous path's enduring advance in light corresponds to the continual light of the righteous, contrasted with the impious person's extinguished light.
Ungodly travelers stumble without knowing how; John describes the person who hates a brother walking in darkness without knowing where he goes because darkness has blinded his eyes.
Applying the ear to the father's words corresponds to the earlier assurance that the ear will obey wisdom and the learner will apply the heart to understanding.
The command to keep the father's words in the heart corresponds to Deuteronomy's placement of God's commanded words in the heart and soul.
The words give life and healing for all flesh; the earlier instruction likewise promises healing for the body and care for the bones.

Proverbs joins guarding the heart to life's outlets, retaining the plural wording 'from these'; Jesus says evil reasonings and deeds come from within people's hearts and defile them. The connection does not resolve the reference of Proverbs' plural 'these'.
Removing a crooked mouth and unjust lips corresponds to the command to stop the tongue from evil and the lips from speaking deceit.
Directing one's eyes toward righteous things corresponds to the psalmist's refusal to place a lawless matter before his eyes.
The instruction to make straight tracks for the feet is repeated in Hebrews' exhortation to make straight tracks so that the lame may be healed rather than dislocated.
The prohibition on turning to the right or the left matches Deuteronomy's command to follow the Lord's instruction without turning either way.

relationship: divine knowledge of the righteous way
rationale: God's knowledge of the right-hand ways, contrasted with perverted left-hand ways, corresponds to the psalm's contrast between the Lord knowing the righteous way and the ungodly way perishing.
God's making tracks straight and advancing the journey is paired with the Lord directing a person's steps and desiring his way.
